content: The order Lamiales is a taxonomic group within the asterid clade of dicotyledonous flowering plants. It encompasses approximately 11,000 species distributed across about 10 families. Prominent members of this order include plants such as lavender, lilac, olive, jasmine, ash tree, teak, snapdragon, and various culinary herbs like mint, basil, and rosemary. Characteristics Plants within the Lamiales order generally exhibit the following morphological traits, although exceptions to these characteristics do exist: The ovary is superior and consists of two carpels that are fused together. The flowers typically have five petals that are fused into a tubular structure. The corollas are bilaterally symmetrical and often bilabiate (two-lipped) in form. There are usually four or fewer fertile stamens present. Taxonomic History Historically, the circumscription of Lamiales was more restricted. For example, under the classification system proposed by Arthur Cronquist, the order included major families such as Lamiaceae (formerly known as Labiatae), Verbenaceae, and Boraginaceae, along with a few smaller families. However, more recent phylogenetic studies have demonstrated that Lamiales, as previously defined, was polyphyletic. This means that the group did not include all descendants of a common ancestor, necessitating a reorganization of its classification. As a result, Lamiales has been expanded to include the former order Scrophulariales, as well as the previously separate orders Hippuridales and Plantaginales. The name Lamiales is now the preferred designation for this larger, more inclusive group. Despite this reclassification, the placement of the family Boraginaceae remains uncertain, as phylogenetic evidence indicates that it does not belong within Lamiales. Additionally, the family Scrophulariaceae, which was historically defined as a paraphyletic group (a group that includes some but not all descendants of a common ancestor), has undergone significant redefinition. This reorganization has led to the creation of several smaller, more clearly defined families that are believed to be monophyletic (containing all descendants of a common ancestor).
